title: perf
summary: Linux's sampling profiler: PMU overflow interrupts and ring buffers, stat vs record vs trace, a 100%-CPU diagnosis with IPC and flame graphs, and the gotchas.

clips.title: How sampling works
clips.question: How does perf profile a program with almost no overhead?

scenes.say: perf, question one. How does perf profile a running program, down to the function, with almost no overhead? Pause and answer out loud.

props.question: How does perf profile with almost no overhead?

scenes.say: The CPU's performance monitoring unit counts an event in hardware: cycles, by default. perf programs the counter to overflow every N events, about four thousand times a second. Each overflow raises a non-maskable interrupt, and the kernel captures the instruction pointer and the call stack, writing the sample into a per-CPU ring buffer. perf record drains that buffer into perf dot data, and perf report symbolizes the samples, or you fold them into a flame graph. Because it samples instead of instrumenting, overhead stays at a few percent. But anything shorter than one sample period can be missed.

steps.note: Overflow every N events (~4 kHz by default)
Statistical: a few % overhead, short functions can hide

scenes.say: perf has three modes. perf stat counts: totals for the whole run, with no attribution and essentially no overhead. perf record samples: periodic stacks, so you know where the time went. And tracing records every occurrence of an event, like each syscall: exact, but expensive.

clips.title: Diagnosing 100% CPU
clips.question: A service is pinned at 100% CPU. How do you diagnose it with perf?

scenes.say: Question two. A service is pinned at one hundred percent CPU. Walk through how you'd diagnose it with perf. Pause and answer out loud.

props.question: A service at 100% CPU: how do you diagnose it?

scenes.say: Start with perf top, attached to the process, for a live view of the hottest symbols. Then count before you sample: perf stat with dash d reports instructions per cycle, and cache and branch misses. An IPC below one means the core is stalling, on memory or on branches, not doing useful work. Next, sample call stacks for thirty seconds, at ninety-nine hertz, an odd rate that avoids lining up with periodic work, and read them in perf report. Finally, fold the stacks into a flame graph: width is time on CPU, height is call depth.

props.title: Count first, then sample
props.code:
# 1. Live view: which symbols are hot right now?
perf top -p $PID

# 2. Counters first: cycles, IPC, cache and branch misses
perf stat -d -p $PID -- sleep 10
#    IPC < 1 → stalled on memory or branches

# 3. Sample call stacks for 30 s at 99 Hz
perf record -F 99 -g -p $PID -- sleep 30
perf report

# 4. Fold the stacks into a flame graph
perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl | flamegraph.pl > flame.svg

scenes.say: Question three. perf says a function is cold, but you know it's slow. Why might perf mislead you? Pause and answer out loud.

Four classic gotchas. perf sees only on-CPU time: a thread blocked on a lock or on I/O is invisible, so use off-CPU analysis, like perf sched, or eBPF. Short or inlined functions hide: they're shorter than a sample period, or their cycles land in the caller. Broken stacks: most distro libraries drop frame pointers, so use DWARF or LBR unwinding. And skid: the sampled instruction can be several past the one that caused the event, so use precise sampling, PEBS, with the colon p p suffix.

items.label: Missing
items.title: Short or inlined
items.body: Below one sample period, or folded into the caller.

items.label: Stacks
items.title: No frame pointers
items.body: Unwind with DWARF or LBR instead.

items.label: Precision
items.title: Skid
items.body: Precise sampling pins the real instruction.

scenes.say: To recap. perf samples hardware counter overflows, with a few percent overhead. Count with perf stat first, and let IPC tell you whether you're stalled. Then sample stacks with perf record, and read a flame graph. And remember it only sees on-CPU time, and statistical samples can miss short work.

items.text: perf stat first: IPC says stalled or busy.
perf record -g, then a flame graph.
On-CPU only; short work can be missed.
